Time-domain reconstruction

Transient excitations (impacts, shocks, transient loads) are naturally described in the time domain. The response of a linear structure is then a convolution of the forces with the impulse responses, which, once discretized, is again a linear problem 𝑦=𝐻𝑢+𝑛.

space–timeMIMO convolutionLpq

The convolution model

With 𝑛𝑡 time steps 𝑡𝑘=(𝑘−1)Δ𝑡, the displacement measured by sensor 𝑖 reads

where ℎ𝑖𝑗 is the impulse response between point 𝑗 and sensor 𝑖. Stacking the time samples gives a block lower-triangular (Toeplitz) matrix 𝐻 of size 𝑛𝑚𝑛𝑡×𝑛𝑟𝑛𝑡, acting on vec(𝑈) where 𝑈 is the 𝑛𝑟×𝑛𝑡 matrix of the forces. For a modal model, ℎ𝑖𝑗(𝑡)=∑𝑛𝜑𝑛(𝑥𝑖)𝜑𝑛(𝑥𝑗)ℎ𝑛(𝑡) where ℎ𝑛 is the impulse response of the 𝑛-th single-degree-of-freedom mode. The modal basis of the steel beam and the impulse responses ℎ𝑛 come from StructuralVibration.jl (impulse_response of a Sdof); the helper convolution_matrix of the documentation (see _lib/setup.jl) assembles them into the matrix 𝐻.

import StructuralVibration as SV
using StructuralVibration: Beam, modefreq, modeshape, agwn

beam = Beam(1.0, 3e-4, 2.5e-9, 2.1e11, 7850.)
t = range(0, 0.06, length = 150)                 # 60 ms, Δt ≈ 0.40 ms
ωn, kn = modefreq(beam, 1 / (2.5 * step(t)))     # modes below fs / 2.5
xm, xr = grid(12), grid(9)
ϕm, ϕr = modeshape(beam, kn, xm), modeshape(beam, kn, xr)

H = convolution_matrix(ωn, 0.01, ϕm, ϕr, t);
@printf "%d modes, H is %d × %d\n" length(ωn) size(H)...

6 modes, H is 1800 × 1350

The reference excitation combines an impact-like pulse at point 3 and a 200 Hz burst at point 7 (displacement measurements, signal-to-noise ratio of 25 dB):

Uref = zeros(length(xr), length(t))
Uref[3, :] .= @. exp(-((t - 0.01) / 0.0015)^2)
Uref[7, :] .= @. 0.6 * sin(2π * 200 * t) * (0.02 < t < 0.04)

Y0 = reshape(H * vec(Uref), length(xm), :)       # nm × nt measurements
Y = agwn(Y0, 25)
prob = InverseProblem(H, Y)

InverseProblem(1800 data, unknown 9×150, DenseOperator)

The measurements are simulated with the same discrete model as the one used for the inversion; the impulse responses are however those of the continuous structure, sampled at the time steps. Since Y is a matrix and H a dense matrix with size(H, 1) == length(Y), the problem is interpreted as a space–time problem: the unknown is a 9 × 150 matrix.

Reconstructions

The Tikhonov solution is compared with the multiplicative regularization using an ℓ1 norm and two mixed norms. In the time domain, Lpq(p, q) couples the time samples of each point: the sources are localized in space (𝑞≤1) and the inner ℓ2 norm does not constrain their time history.

cases = [
    "Tikhonov (GCV)"        => Additive(Lq(2.0); λ = GCV()),
    "Multiplicative ℓ1"     => Multiplicative(Lq(1.0)),
    "Multiplicative ℓ2,1"   => Multiplicative(Lpq(2, 1)),
    "Multiplicative ℓ2,0.5" => Multiplicative(Lpq(2, 0.5)),
]
sols = [name => solve(prob, f) for (name, f) in cases];

fig = Figure(size = (840, 520))
for (k, i) in enumerate((3, 7))
    ax = Axis(fig[k, 1], title = @sprintf("Point %d (x = %.2f m)", i, xr[i]),
              xlabel = k == 2 ? "Time (ms)" : "", ylabel = "Force (N)")
    lines!(ax, 1e3 .* t, Uref[i, :], color = FG, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 2.5, label = "Reference")
    for (name, s) in sols[[1, 4]]
        lines!(ax, 1e3 .* t, s.u[i, :], label = name)
    end
    k == 1 && axislegend(ax, position = :rt)
end
fig

fig = Figure(size = (840, 280))
maps = ["Reference" => Uref, "Tikhonov (GCV)" => last(sols[1]).u, "Multiplicative ℓ2,0.5" => last(sols[4]).u]
for (k, (name, U)) in enumerate(maps)
    ax = Axis(fig[1, k], title = name, xlabel = "Time (ms)", ylabel = k == 1 ? "x (m)" : "")
    heatmap!(ax, 1e3 .* t, xr, transpose(U), colormap = :balance, colorrange = (-1, 1))
end
fig
MethodRelative errorIterations
Tikhonov (GCV)87.2 %0
Multiplicative ℓ191.9 %100
Multiplicative ℓ2,186.4 %100
Multiplicative ℓ2,0.540.5 %47

The quadratic prior spreads the energy of the forces over all the points, while the mixed norm ℓ2,0.5 concentrates it on the two loaded points.

Note
A space–time problem is solved as a whole, with a dense system of size 𝑛𝑟𝑛𝑡. Its cost grows quickly with the number of time steps: for long signals, consider a frequency-domain formulation, or a sparse (assembled) operator if the impulse responses are short.
